title: An attack tool posted online by hackers exposed the full process of an AI-powered attack

content_html:
The hackers’ mistake this time was not that the attack failed, but that they put their tool on the public internet. News on November 23: Amazon’s threat intelligence team disclosed that criminals recently used an autonomous AI platform, Cairn, to attack a medical imaging application and used a zero-day vulnerability to successfully take control of the target server.

Give It the Next Command, and It Gets to Work

Cairn was originally a legitimate automated penetration testing tool, but it has now been weaponized. A zero-day vulnerability is a flaw the vendor has not yet noticed and for which no patch is available. The AI agent took over the entire process: the hacker only issued one instruction—“obtain Shell access”—and it then searched on its own for vulnerable systems exposed to the public internet, trying to seize control one by one. The intrusions occurred from September 8 to 10 and mainly targeted educational institutions in East Asia; Gambit Security also linked it to a credit card theft campaign in September. Amazon was able to trace the attackers because the attackers exposed the Cairn instance directly to the public internet, where anyone could access it.

As Fast as Under 3 Hours, but Not Every Attempt Succeeds

AI is not invincible: when attacking a Redis server, it performed 148 operations in a row and spent more than 16 hours, yet still failed; against a university’s GPU server, it tried more than 30,000 combinations over 6 hours and still could not take it down.

The real change is in speed and scale—the FBI has warned that multiple threat groups are weaponizing such tools, and the finance, government, manufacturing, technology, and healthcare sectors are all within range; in some intrusions, it took less than 3 hours from targeting to obtaining privileged access. Based on this, Amazon recommends that defenders shift to automated systems: security personnel should focus on reviewing system output rather than checking every action one by one. When attacks are handed off to AI agents to run at scale, and defense still relies on humans watching every move, the defenders have already lost on pace.
